title: The wound that starts a war
hookLine: the joking stops when she lunges at Sita, and what follows will start a war
carry: karma: every act is a seed

lines: A METEOR AT A GENTLE STAR.
cards: Sent back and forth between the brothers, laughed at and refused, Shurpanakha turns on the person she blames. It's because of her, she says, looking at Sita. I'll eat her right now, and then you'll be mine.
She rushes at Sita, and Valmiki compares it to a great meteor hurtling toward a gentle star. Sita, who has said nothing through all of this, is terrified. There's no more time for jokes.

teach.h: MARK HER SO SHE CAN'T DO THIS AGAIN.
teach.b: Rama catches her, holds her back, and speaks sharply to Lakshmana. We shouldn't joke with the cruel, he says. Look how close Sita came.
Mark her, so she can't do this again. Lakshmana draws his sword and cuts off her nose and ears. Shurpanakha flees screaming into the forest, to her brother Khara.
It's a violent scene, and hard to sit with.
Some devotional readers see it simply: she tried to kill Sita, and the brothers stopped her without taking her life. Others, especially modern readers, find it harsh, all the more after the teasing.

In some later tellings, like Kamban's Tamil Ramayana and Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, she first comes in a beautiful disguise, and recent writers have retold it from her side. It's fine to hold the discomfort.
Ask most people what karma means and they'll say revenge: she had it coming, so wait and watch. That's not quite the Hindu idea.
Karma means action, and the teaching is that every action is a seed.
It ripens, sometimes slowly, often through many hands, and it binds the one who does it. Watch the Ramayana show it. A proposal, a joke, a lunge, a sword.
The wound goes to Khara. Khara's defeat will go to Lanka. Lanka's pride will go to war.
Many teachers read the forest book this way: nobody's act stays small. And it's why the Bhagavad Gita tells Arjuna to do his work without grasping at the fruit.
Your part is the seed, planted well; the fruit isn't yours to grab.

how: The mutilation of Shurpanakha is staged in Ramlila performances and much discussed in modern retellings, and some teachers use the chain from this hut to the war in Lanka to explain karma.

games.q: someone hurt your friend, and your friend says 'karma will get them.' by the Hindu teaching, what fits?
o: karma is my acts too: what i plant next is my part.
right, karma is the universe's revenge. just wait.
karma is fate, so nothing anyone does matters.
games.why: karma means action. in the Ramayana every act in the scene becomes a seed, and the Gita turns it back on you: tend your own.

practice: Take a pen and a scrap of paper. Write one small thing you did yesterday: a kind word, a favor, a sharp reply. Draw an arrow, and write where it might have traveled: who it reached, who they passed it on to.
No judging, just see the seed and its road, and breathe. If you pray, you might offer today's acts to God, as the Gita asks; if not, simply choose one good seed to plant today.

wordCard.voice: Shurpanakha. She attacks Sita, Lakshmana cuts off her nose and ears, and she flees to Khara. The road to war begins here.

orig.note: Sanskrit janasthāna: the region of Dandaka ruled by Khara, where Shurpanakha runs.

carryVoice: Carry this: karma, every act is a seed. Her wound is already on its way to Khara. See you tomorrow.
